title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM + CUDA graphs - deep dive
summary: Deep technical session reviewing GPU runtime profiling for LumenAI. Covered kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graph warmup behavior, KV cache/ prefix cache effects, batching/throughput strategies, and quantization impact. Customer constraints: VPC/on-prem deployment, KMS, SOC2. Agreed to run targeted benchmarks and share profiling artifacts.

Redwood SE to attach SOC2 + KMS integration docs to the CRM record

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-11
Start time: 17:34 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (SRE - LumenAI), Ben Ortiz (ML Infra), Dr. Chloe Park (CTO)

Auto-generated summary: (may be noisy) deep dive on tensorrt vllm cudagraphs kernel selection and kv cache impacts on latency and throughput.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and Ravi our SE will lead the profiling discussion.
[00:12] Ravi: hi all, thanks. quick agenda: kernel selection, tensorrt-llm vs vLLM perf, cuda graphs warmup and replay, kv cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, then q&a.
[00:30] Aisha: thanks. we're primarily interested in on-prem / VPC deployment performance. we have A100 nodes and some 80GB A100s in staging. main ask: can you show where tensorrt helps vs vllm for our 8k and 32k contexts?
[00:48] Ben: also cost — we run heavy embedding/ generation loads, so throughput per GPU matters. we care about latency p50 and p95 for sync endpoints.
[01:05] Ravi: got it. quick context: in our tests tensorrt-llm's kernel fusion + cudagraphs usually gives better steady-state throughput for long-context FP16 workloads, whereas vLLM is often better at low-latency single-request scenarios with small batches because of its scheduling. but there are a lot of caveats.
[01:30] Chloe: caveats like?
[01:32] Ravi: warmup for cuda graphs, kernel selection heuristics — if sequence lengths vary a lot, the compiled kernels for one bucket might be suboptimal for another; and quantization interactions with tensorrt can change perf. also kv cache eviction and prefix reuse matter a lot.
[01:50] Aisha: can you show numbers? rough ballpark is fine.
[01:54] Ravi: sure — rough from our internal: for a 13B model on an A100 80GB with FP16 + TensorRT-LLM + CUDA graphs, steady throughput at batch 8 and 8k context was about 900–1200 tok/s. vLLM on the same node with optimized scheduling and CPU offload did about 600–900 tok/s in our run but with lower p50 latency at batch 1. again approximate.
[02:20] Ben: so tensorrt is 1.3–1.6x faster on throughput in that case?
[02:23] Ravi: yes for that specific config. but if you go to int8 quantization path in tensorrt, you can get further improvements, sometimes 1.8x, but accuracy/regression risk increases.
[02:40] Maya: also note that kernel selection varies by sequence bucket. our runtime picks kernels based on model arch, context length histogram, and hardware. for mixed sequence lengths you may prefer vLLM-style dynamic scheduling unless you have strong prefix caching.
[03:00] Aisha: tell us more about the KV/prefix cache. we saw big latency hits when we lost the prefix.
[03:07] Ravi: yes, KV cache is critical. when the KV cache is hot (prefix reuse across requests), you avoid re-computing early layers and get huge p50 improvements. our platform supports persistent prefix caches and cross-request KV reuse for customer workloads, but on on-prem you need to configure memory pinning and GPU memory reservation. if the cache thrashes — e.g., many unique prefixes — throughput and latency suffer.
[03:36] Ben: what's the memory overhead?
[03:38] Ravi: for 8k context KV, for a 13B model you might need ~20–30GB of GPU memory for cached KV per attention head state depending on implementation; we usually recommend reserving headroom and using sharding if needed.
[03:55] Aisha: okay. about cudagraphs: we've seen warmup spikes where first few requests are slow. is that expected?
[04:02] Ravi: yes — cudagraph capture and replay helps reduce kernel launch overhead, but initial captures can be expensive. our recommendation: use stable-length buckets or pre-warm graphs with representative traces — we typically run a brief trace phase at deployment to capture common paths. that reduces p95 after warmup.
[04:20] Chloe: does tensorrt-llm require re-compilation for each model version?
[04:24] Ravi: there's usually a one-time compile/optimization step for a model binary variant (FP16/int8) and for each context length bucket. compilation takes minutes to an hour depending on hardware. we surface prebuilt variants for common open models to speed onboarding.
[04:40] Ben: what about failsafe? if the compiled graph fails due to a new prompt shape do you fallback?
[04:46] Ravi: yes we fall back to a safe interpreter path or to a vLLM-compatible runtime for that request, so you avoid downtime but pay latency cost. we also maintain multiple kernel variants and a routing policy.
[05:00] Maya: quick poll — are you more concerned about peak throughput or latency SLO today?
[05:05] Aisha: latency p95 for interactive products is the priority, but throughput is crucial for batch jobs.
[05:10] Chloe: we need predictable cost for forecasting as well.
[05:13] Ravi: then a hybrid approach is often best: serve interactive endpoints on a smaller vLLM-optimized fleet or tensorrt variants with aggressive caching, and route batch workloads to dedicated tensorrt pools.
[05:30] Aisha: about quantization — you mentioned int8 can be risky. our models have safety/accuracy constraints. how do you measure regressions?
[05:39] Ravi: we run golden prompt sets and n-gram/embedding distance checks and have regression thresholds. we can run evals on your prompts. int8 can introduce hallucination or shift in probability mass especially for instruction-heavy prompts; often per-layer calibration and selective quantization (only FFN or attention) mitigates risk.
[06:05] Ben: any tips for kernel selection tuning?
[06:08] Ravi: collect a distribution of sequence lengths and token generation patterns, then prioritize kernels for the top N buckets. also ensure your batching policy is aware of latency SLOs — e.g., don't wait to fill batch if p95 must be low. our runtime has adaptive batching with a max-latency gating parameter.
[06:30] Aisha: can we see a trace?
[06:33] Ravi: yes — I'm pulling up a recent trace from our internal profiling. note: this was on an A100 80GB, 13B model, batch 4, 8k context.
[06:42] [Ravi shares link: /redwood/profiles/trace-2026-11-30.zip] (link is placeholder)
[06:48] Ravi: you'll see large spikes during graph capture at ~00:06 in that trace, then steady-state after 30s. the kernel timeline shows fused attention kernels dominating runtime. there's a kernel selection event where we pick a different matmul configuration at 00:12 for shorter sequences.
[07:10] Chloe: are these traces reproducible in our on-prem? we can't share production data but can run on staging.
[07:16] Ravi: yes — we can provide a docker image and script to run the same tracing. we'll need access to a staging GPU with similar specs.
[07:25] Aisha: security question — if you run profiling on our nodes, how does key management work?
[07:30] Maya: we support KMS integrations and never persist customer keys in our control plane for private deployments. for dedicated or private we can run the profiling tooling as a container you control, and logs can be pushed to your S3/vault. we'll attach SOC2 docs.
[07:49] Ben: good. back to performance — what about multi-GPU sharding for 70B models? we plan to test larger models later.
[07:58] Ravi: multi-GPU is more complex: tensor parallel kernels and KV distribution add cross-GPU comms overhead. TensorRT-LLM supports model-parallel fusion but network topology matters. for now let's focus on 13B/33B class single-node sharding; we can schedule a separate session for 70B+ with TP/PP details.
[08:20] Aisha: in the trace you mentioned fused attention — are those custom kernels or vendor-supplied?
[08:24] Ravi: mostly vendor kernels (cuBLAS/cuDNN) with some custom fused attention shipped in the TensorRT-LLM path. our runtime picks between custom fusions and vendor matmul depending on input sizes. sometimes vendor library updates change perf — we track that and have kernel blacklists if a vendor update regresses performance.
[08:48] Ben: what's the typical p95 improvement after you pre-warm graphs?
[08:52] Ravi: depends, but we've seen p95 drop from 700ms to 220ms after capture and warmup for certain configs. your mileage varies.
[09:03] Chloe: can you quantify tail risk if KV cache is cold? like worst-case p95?
[09:07] Ravi: if the KV cache is cold and you don't have cudagraphs, p95 can spike several seconds for long contexts because you're re-running earlier tokens. with capture+cache we bring that down substantially.
[09:20] Aisha: regarding batching — do you recommend dynamic batching on on-prem?
[09:24] Ravi: dynamic batching is good but set the latency ceiling. we support latency-first batching where the system will push a partial batch when latency threshold is reached. For throughput-heavy workloads, increase max batch size and use background warmup requests.
[09:40] Ben: how do you instrument to measure per-kernel time? we want flame graphs for GPUs.
[09:44] Ravi: we use nvprof/nvtx annotations and CUPTI traces and convert to flame timelines. we then aggregate per-kernel durations. we'll share example traces.
[09:55] Chloe: any gotchas with CUDA graph replay and dynamic sequence lengths?
[09:58] Ravi: yes — graphs assume a static sequence shape; for dynamic we maintain multiple graphs per bucket. if you have huge variability you can fallback to the interpreter or JIT compile on the fly but that adds overhead.
[10:15] Aisha: about quantization again — do you support mixed precision per-layer?
[10:19] Ravi: yes, selective quantization is supported. we can quantize FFN to int8 while keeping attention in FP16 to maintain fidelity. that's usually safer.
[10:30] Ben: do you have automated eval pipelines for checking generation quality after quantization?
[10:33] Ravi: yes — we can run A/B evals across your prompt set, measuring embedding distances, BLEU-style heuristics, and token-level distribution shifts.
[10:45] Chloe: let's talk about timeline — we want to pilot in Jan. what's a realistic plan?
[10:50] Maya: pilot sequence: week 1 — share prompts and staging access; week 2 — Redwood runs profiling and shares logs and recommended config; week 3 — run a small pilot with 1-2 dedicated GPUs and validated correctness; week 4 — expand or tune.
[11:06] Aisha: sounds good. about cost — can you give rough cost delta between hosted and dedicated?
[11:10] Maya: ballpark: hosted is pay-as-you-go; dedicated has lower per-token cost at scale but requires commit. I'll send a tiered pricing sheet.
[11:18] Ben: technical question — how do you handle checkpointing KV cache across restarts?
[11:22] Ravi: for private deployments we persist KV to local NVMe with encryption and rehydrate on restart; for hosted we keep in-memory with TTLs but support snapshot/rehydrate to S3 for cold-start acceleration.
[11:36] Chloe: does snapshotting add latency?
[11:38] Ravi: snapshot/restore cost is amortized; we usually snapshot asynchronously and only restore hot prefixes when needed.
[11:46] Aisha: any recommendations for our 32k experiments? we plan to test 32k context with long docs.
[11:51] Ravi: 32k is a different regime: memory pressure is large, kv sharding and offloading strategies matter. tensorrt-llm can handle it if you have 80GB+ and adjust chunking; you might need to use recompute or activation partitioning. Also watch pmem vs gpu memory tradeoffs.
[12:10] Ben: what about using NVLink vs PCIe for multi-GPU?
[12:13] Ravi: NVLink is strongly preferred for multi-GPU KV sharing and lowers interconnect latency. PCIe can work but adds frictions at scale.
[12:25] Chloe: any real-world regression case you can share?
[12:28] Ravi: we had a case where a vendor driver update changed matmul heuristics and regressed a specific kernel; we rolled back vendor lib and blacklisted the bad kernel until fixed. implies you should include library-version pinning in your onboarding checklist.
[12:46] Aisha: ok that's helpful. can you outline the exact artifacts you'll share?
[12:50] Maya: sure — benchmark spreadsheet with raw tok/s and latency numbers, nvprof/CUPTI trace zips, example cudagraph capture logs, recommended config yaml for your staging, SOC2 + KMS integration guide, and a short runbook for warmup.
[13:05] Ben: timeline for those?
[13:08] Maya: I'll send the pricing and runbook by Monday (2026-12-13). Ravi will run the profiling week of 12/14 and share traces by 12/18.

[13:22] Aisha: yes we'll try to get that by EOW.
[13:26] Chloe: last question — do you support single-tenant encrypted in-VPC control plane?
[13:30] Maya: yes that's part of our Private offering, we'll include architecture notes in the docs.
[13:38] Aisha: cool thanks.

[14:10] Ben: any recommended thresholds for switching kernels?
[14:13] Ravi: we switch based on microbenchmarks per shape — if one kernel is 1.1x faster across multiple runs we pick it; we also penalize high variance kernels.
